sources.title: Report of the Committee to develop a Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence (FREE-AI) in the Financial Sector
sources.note: RBI committee report. It sets 7 foundational Sutras, 26 recommendations and six strategic pillars for responsible AI adoption in finance.

sources.title: Reserve Bank of India Annual Report 2024-25 - Regulation, Supervision and Financial Stability
sources.note: Primary RBI annual-report chapter covering AI in complaint management, supervisory technology, fraud detection and the FREE-AI programme.

sources.title: RBI Bulletin - Developmental and Regulatory Policies: FREE-AI and MuleHunter.AI
sources.note: Primary RBI policy statement describing the MuleHunter.AI pilot and the rationale for a responsible-AI framework.

sources.title: RBI draft Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management
sources.note: Primary RBI press release for draft guidance. It applies to all models used by covered regulated entities, including third-party and AI/ML models. The guidance was released for public comment and is not presented here as final regulation.

sources.title: SEBI Board Memorandum - Assigning responsibility for use of AI tools by regulated persons
sources.note: Primary SEBI board material listing observed AI/ML use cases across brokers, depositories, market infrastructure institutions and mutual funds.

sources.title: SEBI (Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025 - responsibility for AI use
sources.note: Final SEBI regulation making covered intermediaries solely responsible for data privacy/security/integrity, AI outputs they rely on, and compliance with law.

sources.title: SEBI Consultation Paper - Guidelines for Responsible Usage of AI/ML in Indian Securities Markets
sources.note: Primary SEBI consultation paper documenting current market use cases and proposed responsible-AI principles. It is a consultation paper, not final regulation.

sources.title: SEBI Guidelines for Investment Advisers
sources.note: Primary SEBI circular requiring advisers using AI tools to remain responsible for client data, information used, AI-based advice and legal compliance, and to disclose the extent of AI use.

sources.title: Bajaj Finserv Limited - 19th Annual Report 2025-26
sources.note: Company-reported operating metrics for AI-enabled servicing, lending, document processing, voice-to-data conversion and claims automation. Metrics are reported by Bajaj Finserv and are not independently verified by MarketDeck.

sources.title: Axis Bank Integrated Annual Report 2024-25
sources.note: Company-reported deployment of Axis Deep Intelligence, a GenAI internal assistant across 5,500+ branches supporting 100,000+ employees.

pages.title: AI in Indian Finance
pages.intro: Where it is actually creating value - and why the important boundary is not AI versus humans, but assistance versus delegated authority.

sections.title: The working thesis
sections.text: The most defensible near-term value is showing up in workflow compression: service, document processing, fraud detection, risk support, research and operations. The higher the consequence of an automated decision, the stronger the case for provenance, human review and clear accountability.

pages.callout: Published 28 September 2026. Research and education only. This issue does not provide investment, credit or legal advice.

pages.title: Useful AI is mostly workflow AI
pages.intro: Ignore the science-fiction framing. In Indian finance, the practical story is already visible in the operating layer.

sections.title: Five places to look
items: Customer service: faster routing, retrieval and first-line resolution.
Fraud and surveillance: pattern detection that narrows what humans need to inspect.
Lending and credit: document processing and decision support around underwriting.
Research and compliance: summarisation, monitoring, document review and analyst assistance.
Operations: reconciliation, claims, voice-to-data conversion and employee copilots.

sections.title: The control question
sections.text: Automation can reduce friction without removing accountability. This issue separates low-consequence assistance from decisions that can deny credit, freeze money, shape advice or materially affect a customer. [S4] [S6] [S8]

sections.title: Evidence note
sections.text: Regulatory documents are treated as primary policy evidence. Company annual reports are used only for clearly labelled company-reported operating metrics. Drafts and consultations are labelled as drafts or consultations, not final rules.

pages.callout: Read the issue as a map of value plus control: what AI can accelerate, what must remain reviewable, and who remains responsible.

pages.title: Five workflows, one pattern
pages.intro: The recurring pattern is not autonomous finance. It is AI reducing the amount of information a person or system must manually process before the next decision.

sections.title: The useful middle
sections.text: SEBI's own inventory of market use cases includes surveillance, KYC/AML, risk management, data analysis, document review, cyber security, customer service and chatbots. RBI examples include fraud detection and complaint handling. [S2] [S5] [S7]

sections.title: Where value compounds
sections.text: AI becomes more useful when the input is high-volume, repetitive and reviewable: documents, conversations, transaction patterns, complaints, filings and internal knowledge. That does not make the downstream decision low-risk.

sections.title: What this chart is - and is not
sections.text: The visual is a MarketDeck workflow map, not a ranking of returns or an estimate of market size. It shows where primary sources document actual use or deployment.

pages.callout: Editorial takeaway: the strongest evidence today is around throughput and decision support, not autonomous financial judgment.
pages.figureAlt: Editorial workflow map of five AI use-case lanes in Indian finance, from service to operations.
pages.figureCaption: MarketDeck editorial schematic; use-case evidence is cited in the surrounding text.

pages.title: The first win is response capacity
pages.intro: Service is a natural entry point because a bot can retrieve, classify and resolve routine work while preserving an escalation path for higher-stakes cases.

sections.title: A concrete operating metric
sections.text: Bajaj Finserv reports that 65% of customer servicing at Bajaj Finance was handled through AI voice and text bots in FY2026. It also reports that Bajaj Finserv Health resolved about 55% of customer queries using agentic AI. These are company-reported operating metrics, not independent quality scores. [S9]

sections.title: The regulator is experimenting too
sections.text: RBI's 2024-25 Annual Report says it is working with ReBIT to integrate AI into the Complaint Management System in phases: phase I for a conversational AI chatbot for complainants, followed by more advanced complaint-processing features. [S2]

sections.title: Design the handoff, not just the bot
sections.text: A service system should know when it is answering a routine question, when it is interpreting a rule, and when the customer needs a human. The practical KPI is not simply containment rate; it is resolution quality with a reliable escalation path.

pages.callout: Good service AI reduces waiting and repetitive work. It should not make a difficult complaint harder to reach a human with.
pages.figureAlt: Company-reported FY2026 customer-service metrics from Bajaj Finserv businesses, shown with separate denominators.
pages.figureCaption: Company-reported operating metrics from Bajaj Finserv Limited; not independent quality scores.

pages.title: AI is useful when it narrows the haystack
pages.intro: Fraud systems are a strong fit for machine learning because the first job is often to surface unusual behaviour quickly - not to declare guilt.

sections.title: MuleHunter.AI is a useful example
sections.text: RBI described MuleHunter.AI, developed by RBI Innovation Hub, as an AI/ML model for detecting mule bank accounts more efficiently. A pilot with two large public sector banks produced encouraging results, and banks were encouraged to collaborate further. [S3]

sections.title: Surveillance is already a securities-market use case
sections.text: SEBI's board material lists surveillance, KYC/AML, risk management, behaviour analysis and cyber security among observed AI/ML uses across brokers, depositories, market infrastructure institutions and mutual funds. [S5]

sections.title: The decision boundary matters
sections.text: A model can rank suspicious accounts or transactions without becoming the final authority. False positives have real costs: blocked payments, delayed access, additional verification and customer distress. The higher the impact, the stronger the case for documented review and redress.

pages.callout: Detection is not adjudication. The safest architecture separates anomaly scoring from the decision that affects the customer.
pages.figureAlt: Schematic separating fraud detection and triage from human review and downstream action.
pages.figureCaption: MarketDeck editorial schematic illustrating a reviewable fraud-control workflow.

pages.title: Faster underwriting is valuable - but consequential
pages.intro: Lending combines exactly what AI likes - documents, repeated decisions and large datasets - with exactly what governance worries about: fairness, explainability and access to credit.

sections.title: AI is already connected to loan workflows
sections.text: Bajaj Finserv reports Rs 5,520 crore of conversational-AI-enabled loan disbursals at Bajaj Finance in FY2026 and more than 69 million application documents processed using Vision AI. 'AI-enabled' should not be read as 'AI made the credit decision by itself'. [S9]

sections.title: Document automation is not the same as credit judgment
sections.text: Extracting data from applications, checking completeness and routing cases can remove manual work. Credit approval, pricing and adverse decisions introduce different risks because model errors can directly change a customer's access to finance.

sections.title: Model risk is moving to the centre
sections.text: RBI's June 2026 draft model-risk guidance expands the frame beyond credit models to all models used by covered regulated entities, including third-party and AI/ML models, across the model lifecycle. The document is a draft released for consultation, not final regulation. [S4]

pages.callout: The more a model changes a customer's economic outcome, the less adequate 'the model said so' becomes as an explanation.
pages.figureAlt: Bajaj Finance company-reported FY2026 AI-enabled loan and document-processing metrics alongside a consequence gradient.
pages.figureCaption: Company-reported operating metrics; AI-enabled does not mean autonomous credit approval.

pages.title: AI can compress research; responsibility does not compress
pages.intro: Financial research is a high-leverage use case because models can search, summarise and compare. But the output can travel into advice, execution and compliance decisions.

sections.title: SEBI documents broad use across the market
sections.text: SEBI's 2025 consultation paper records AI/ML use by exchanges for surveillance, cyber security, member support and data automation; by brokers for KYC/document processing, recommendations, chatbots, account opening, surveillance, AML and order execution; and by mutual funds for customer support, surveillance, cyber security and segmentation. [S7]

sections.title: Accountability follows the regulated activity
sections.text: SEBI's 2025 Intermediaries Amendment Regulations make covered regulated persons solely responsible for investor and stakeholder data, the outputs from AI/ML tools they rely on, and compliance with applicable law - whether the tools are built internally or sourced from third parties. [S6]

sections.title: Advice adds disclosure duties
sections.text: SEBI's January 2025 investment-adviser guidelines state that advisers using AI tools remain responsible for client data, other information used to arrive at advice, AI-based advice and legal compliance, and must disclose the extent of AI use to clients. [S8]

pages.callout: AI may shorten the path from document to insight. It does not outsource fiduciary or regulatory responsibility.
pages.figureAlt: Matrix of AI and ML use cases documented by SEBI across exchanges, brokers and mutual funds.
pages.figureCaption: Use cases are summarised from SEBI primary materials cited in the surrounding text.

pages.title: The quiet gains are in the back office
pages.intro: Operations is where AI can create large cumulative value without needing to pretend it can forecast markets.

sections.title: Voice and documents become structured data
sections.text: Bajaj Finserv reports 52 million voice-to-data conversions for customer conversations at Bajaj Finance in FY2026, alongside more than 69 million application documents processed using Vision AI. [S9]

sections.title: Claims and servicing become more automatable
sections.text: The same annual report says Bajaj General expects about a 67% reduction in turnaround time for motor claims through automated invoice processing. Because the figure is explicitly an expected reduction, this issue does not present it as an achieved outcome. [S9]

sections.title: Internal copilots can scale institutional knowledge
sections.text: Axis Bank's FY2024-25 annual report says Axis Deep Intelligence, its GenAI internal chatbot, was deployed across more than 5,500 branches and supported more than 100,000 employees. That is an internal productivity deployment, not a claim about investment returns or customer outcomes. [S10]

pages.callout: The back office is a powerful proving ground: repetitive enough to automate, structured enough to measure, and close enough to human review to recover from errors.
pages.figureAlt: Selected company-reported operating metrics for voice-to-data, document processing and Axis Bank's internal GenAI deployment.
pages.figureCaption: Company-reported deployment scale; not investment-performance evidence.

pages.title: Enable innovation, keep responsibility visible
pages.intro: India's current policy direction is not a simple ban-or-permit choice. It increasingly combines encouragement of AI adoption with explicit responsibility for outcomes.

sections.title: FREE-AI is a framework, not a marketing slogan
sections.text: RBI's FREE-AI committee report sets seven foundational Sutras, 26 actionable recommendations and six strategic pillars. The RBI says the aim is to encourage innovation in harmony with risk mitigation. [S1]

sections.title: SEBI puts responsibility on the regulated person
sections.text: Under SEBI's 2025 Intermediaries Amendment Regulations, covered intermediaries remain responsible for data privacy/security/integrity, AI outputs they use, and legal compliance even when technology is procured from a third party. [S6]

sections.title: Policy status matters
sections.text: The FREE-AI report is a committee framework. SEBI's responsible-AI paper is a consultation paper. RBI's 2026 model-risk guidance is a draft. This issue labels each accordingly and does not describe proposals as binding final rules. [S1] [S4] [S7]

pages.callout: The emerging principle is durable: innovation can be delegated to tools; accountability cannot be delegated away.
pages.figureAlt: Editorial simplification of RBI FREE-AI: enabling pillars and governance pillars, anchored by seven Sutras.
pages.figureCaption: MarketDeck schematic based on the RBI FREE-AI committee report; see source S1.

pages.title: The hard problem begins when the model can act
pages.intro: A summariser and an autonomous decision engine should not share the same control model. Consequence should determine governance.

sections.title: RBI is broadening the model-risk lens
sections.text: RBI's June 2026 draft guidance covers governance, risk tiering, lifecycle management, validation, continuous oversight, change management and business continuity across models used by covered regulated entities, including third-party and AI/ML models. [S4]

sections.title: Think in levels of authority
items: Assist: retrieve, classify, summarise or draft. A human remains the decision-maker.
Recommend: score, rank or propose an action. Human review is explicit for material outcomes.
Act within bounds: execute only inside predetermined limits with logs, overrides and monitoring.
High-impact autonomous action: demands the strongest evidence, controls, accountability and redress.

sections.title: Explainability is a control surface
sections.text: The right explanation depends on the use case. A customer may need the reason an adverse decision occurred; a model-risk team needs reproducibility, validation and monitoring; an operations team needs failure modes and a rollback path. One generic 'AI explanation' cannot serve all three.

pages.callout: A useful rule: as reversibility falls and customer impact rises, human oversight and evidence requirements should rise with it.
pages.figureAlt: MarketDeck authority ladder from assistive AI to high-impact autonomous financial action.
pages.figureCaption: Editorial control framework: oversight should increase as authority and consequence rise.

pages.title: Before automating a financial decision
pages.intro: Use this page as a research worksheet. The goal is not to slow every deployment; it is to make authority, evidence and recovery explicit before the system goes live.

sections.title: Eight questions
items: What exact task is the model performing - retrieval, recommendation or action?
What data is it allowed to use, and what is the provenance and freshness of that data?
What financial or customer consequence can follow from a wrong output?
Who owns the decision and who can override it?
What explanation is required for staff, auditors, regulators and customers?
How are bias, drift, edge cases and adversarial inputs tested?
What is monitored after deployment, and what triggers rollback or shutdown?
What grievance or human-review path exists for an affected customer?

sections.title: The operating principle
sections.text: Do not evaluate only model accuracy. Evaluate the complete decision system: data, model, tools, people, controls, interfaces, monitoring and recovery.

pages.callout: A production AI system is a socio-technical control loop. Governance belongs around the whole loop, not only around the model.

pages.title: Primary sources first
pages.intro: Every material claim in this issue traces to a regulator document or a clearly labelled company annual report.

sections.title: How evidence was handled
sections.text: RBI and SEBI publications are treated as primary policy sources. Company annual reports are used for company-reported operating metrics and are not independently verified by MarketDeck. No company metric is used as proof that one AI system is superior to another.

sections.title: Status labels are part of the evidence
sections.text: A committee report, consultation paper and draft guidance are identified as such. They are not described as final binding rules unless the cited source is a final regulation or circular.

sections.title: No investment conclusion
sections.text: This issue evaluates operating use cases, controls and governance. It does not recommend securities, lenders, banks, fintechs or AI vendors and does not estimate investment returns from AI adoption.

pages.callout: Source review completed 28 September 2026. Recheck regulatory status before relying on any draft or consultation as current law.
